details: picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data manipulation, data exfiltration, denial of service (DoS) by deleting all data, breaches in multi-tenant security environments, and data integrity issues. cna.title: Forged signed tokens let any registered user take over other users and organizations

descriptions.value:
Postiz signs its session, invitation and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without any marker of what a token is for. A route that refreshes the credentials of a browser-extension channel signed data taken from the request itself and stored the result where the requesting user can read it back. A user could therefore obtain a validly signed token containing any claims they choose, which the application accepts as a session, as an organization invitation with a chosen role, as a password reset or as an enterprise provisioning token.

A second, narrower route that creates team invitations signs extra fields from the request body in the same way.

workarounds.value: If you do not use channels that rely on the Postiz browser extension, block POST /integrations/extension-refresh at your reverse proxy. This removes the main signing route; the team invitation route remains.
Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true. The attacker needs an ordinary account, so closing self-registration limits exposure to people who already hold one. This reduces reach, it does not close the issue.

exploits.value: Exploitation was demonstrated end to end against an unmodified backend build at commit 3a7d28b7ad96: a second self-registered user became super administrator of another user's organization and read its API key. Session, password reset, enterprise and subscription tokens obtained the same way were each accepted by their endpoints.

configurations.value: The instance must be able to reach api2.skool.com, as any instance using the Skool provider can. No setting has to be changed.

With Stripe billing configured, the attacker's own plan must allow one channel and the target organization must not be on the STANDARD tier. The session and password reset tokens are not affected by these limits.
Self-registration is open unless DISABLE_REGISTRATION is set to true.

descriptions.value: A registered user can obtain a validly signed token with claims of their choosing and use it as a login session for another user, without knowing any identifier of the victim when database filter objects are used as claims.

An attacker can join any other organization as super administrator, using an organization id that is exposed by any shared post preview link, read its API key and channel list and schedule posts through its connected social accounts.
An attacker can reset the password of a user whose id they know, and can obtain an organization with a lifetime top-tier subscription through the enterprise provisioning endpoint.
Forged tokens do not expire and cannot be told apart from genuine ones.
The narrower invitation route lets a user who may invite team members repeatedly stop the scheduled posts of a channel of another organization, and lift the channel limit of their own plan.

timeline.value: Anthropic has disclosed a thorough report of this vulnerability including a working PoC to Postiz
Postiz has reproduced the vulnerability and is working on a fix
Postiz has pushed a fix for this vulnerability and verified it
Postiz has created a release and published the advisory

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

If a packet with bad checksum metadata gets into the ipv4 stack,
skb_checksum_help can corrupt the network header and cause a bunch of
mischief.

This was discovered and reported by Paulos, and has been reporoduced
by others independently since.

We really shouldn't allow such packets in, but as a defence
in depth measure, let's also check before we complete the checksum.

A more complete validation at input is forthcoming, but needs more work.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A malicious microVM supplies crafted virtio-net checksum metadata with its outbound frame. The VMM writes it to the host TAP, where tun_get_user() feeds the skb to the IPv4 stack and ip_do_fragment() calls skb_checksum_help(); this is a guest/local virtual-device path, not an Internet receive path.
AC:L - The guest controls the frame, checksum start and offset, and packet size and can repeat the same fragmentation sequence. No race, timing window, or uncontrollable memory layout is needed; host leak, crash, and code-execution variants were reproduced with crafted packets.
PR:N - In the microVM scenario, a tenant workload able to transmit through its assigned virtio-net interface can supply the triggering traffic. It needs no host credentials, capability, or access to /dev/net/tun; the privileged VMM merely forwards guest output to its existing TAP fd.
UI:N - The attacker sends the crafted guest packets directly, and host TAP/IPv4 processing invokes checksum completion automatically. No host administrator or other victim must act.
S:C - The checksum metadata originates in an untrusted microVM, but skb_checksum_help() and ip_do_fragment() process and corrupt state in the host kernel. The demonstrated leak, crash, and administrator code execution cross the guest-to-host isolation boundary.
C:H - After skb_checksum_help() changes an already-validated IPv4 IHL, ip_do_fragment() trusts the new length and ip_frag_next() copies beyond the skb's logical linear head into transmitted IPv4 options. This was demonstrated as continuous host-memory disclosure in guest-emitted packets.
I:H - skb_checksum_help() writes at the attacker-controlled checksum position inside an IPv4 header after routing and validation, and downstream code trusts the modified fields. Crafted guest packets using this flaw were demonstrated to execute commands with full administrator privileges on the host.
A:H - Malformed checksum offsets reach skb_checksum_help() from IPv4 fragmentation and can trip WARN_ONCE/panic paths or poison the header geometry used downstream. Crafted guest packets were demonstrated to crash the physical host, taking down all sandboxes on it.

cna.title: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix heap out-of-bounds write in krb5_authenticate()

In krb5_authenticate(), out_len is calculated to determine available
headroom in response_buf for the incoming Kerberos AP-REP token. However,
when SMB2_SESSION_SETUP is processed as a non-first element of a compounded
SMB2 request, the calculation omits work->next_smb2_rsp_hdr_off.

This causes out_len to overstate remaining buffer headroom by
the cumulative size of prior responses in the compound chain. Consequently,
the length check in ksmbd_krb5_authenticate()
(*out_len <= resp->spnego_blob_len) passes erroneously, allowing memcpy()
to write the AP-REP blob past the end of response_buf into adjacent kernel
heap memory.

Fix this by subtracting work->next_smb2_rsp_hdr_off when computing out_len,
ensuring it accurately reflects physical remaining buffer space.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - ksmbd_conn_handler_loop() receives the compound request over TCP/445, and __process_request() dispatches its non-first SMB2 SESSION_SETUP to smb2_sess_setup() and krb5_authenticate(). The SESSION_SETUP SecurityBuffer carries the Kerberos AP-REQ that produces the AP-REP copied by the patched path.
AC:L - The same authenticated peer can create directory entries, request a sized QUERY_DIRECTORY response, and place SESSION_SETUP later in the compound, controlling next_smb2_rsp_hdr_off before supplying its valid AP-REQ; no race or external actor is required.
PR:L - ksmbd_krb5_authenticate() checks KSMBD_USER_FLAG_OK before its length check and memcpy; ksmbd.mountd sets it only after krb5_rd_req() accepts the AP-REQ and usm_handle_login_request() recognizes the account. An ordinary valid Kerberos account suffices, but an unauthenticated peer cannot reach the write.
UI:N - The peer opens the session, prepares the prior compound response, and sends the Kerberos SESSION_SETUP itself; no victim user must open, mount, or approve anything.
S:U - ksmbd_krb5_authenticate() corrupts memory adjacent to the host kernel's response_buf allocation; this remains within the same kernel security authority and crosses no VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary.
C:H - The AP-REP memcpy in ksmbd_krb5_authenticate() can overrun response_buf and corrupt adjacent heap objects; exploitable kernel heap corruption can be converted into a memory-read primitive exposing arbitrary kernel data.
I:H - The memcpy writes resp->spnego_blob_len AP-REP bytes beyond response_buf into adjacent kernel heap memory, enabling corruption of object metadata or control data and potential kernel code execution.
A:H - Writing the AP-REP beyond response_buf can corrupt adjacent allocations or allocator metadata and trigger KASAN, an oops, or a kernel panic; the authenticated SMB peer can repeat the compound request.

cna.title: ksmbd: fix heap out-of-bounds write in krb5_authenticate()

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Use active memslots for the per-vCPU MMIO cache

KVM tags the per-vCPU MMIO cache with a memslot generation so that a
memslot update invalidates cached MMIO information.  Both the fill and
validation paths use kvm_memslots(), which unconditionally selects address
space 0, even when the vCPU is running in SMM and using address space 1.

Commit 56f17dd3fbc4 ("kvm: x86: fix stale mmio cache bug") added the
memslot generation to the cache key so that a memslot update could not
leave a stale entry valid.  When commit 699023e23965 ("KVM: x86: add SMM
to the MMU role, support SMRAM address space") added the SMM address space,
these helpers were not converted to use the active memslots.

Consequently, an update to the SMM memslots can leave an entry from the old
SMM address space apparently valid after the vCPU returns to the normal
address space.  A guest can then cause an access to valid RAM at the same
GFN to be returned to userspace as KVM_EXIT_MMIO.

Completing that exit through the VMM's RAM address space writes the backing
page without going through KVM's write-tracking path.  If the page backs a
nested EPT table, KVM can continue using shadow translations derived from
the old contents.  The WARN_ON_ONCE() in kvm_mmu_write_protect_fault()
catches this invalid cache and memslot combination.

Use the vCPU's active memslots when caching and validating the entry.
Memslot generations are unique across address spaces, so the generation
also distinguishes the normal and SMM views.  This matches the MMIO SPTE
cache, which already uses kvm_vcpu_memslots().

On an unpatched current-mainline kernel, a regression test that fills the
cache in SMM and updates only the SMM memslots fails the intended RAM write
and triggers the kvm_mmu_write_protect_fault() warning.  With this change,
the same test completes the RAM write without a warning.  The x86/smm_test,
set_memory_region_test, and memslot_modification_stress_test selftests also
pass.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The attacker drives guest memory accesses through KVM_RUN via kvm_vcpu_ioctl()->kvm_arch_vcpu_ioctl_run()->handle_ept_violation()/handle_ept_misconfig()->kvm_mmu_page_fault(), reaching the patched MMIO-cache helpers; no network protocol carries the input.
AC:L - A malicious L1 can deterministically enter SMM, fault on an unmapped GFN to fill the cache, alter Q35 SMRAM mappings, execute RSM, and write the same GFN; this requires no race, and the complete sequence was reproduced with nested VMX/EPT.
PR:L - The demonstrated escape needs kernel-level control of the L1 guest to manage SMM and EPT12, but that is tenant-granted guest privilege relative to host KVM; neither kvm_mmu_page_fault() nor vcpu_match_mmio_gen() requires host administrative capability.
UI:N - The malicious L1 performs the SMM access, Q35 SMRAM reconfiguration, RSM, nested-EPT update, and final RAM write itself, without any action by a host user or administrator.
S:C - The flaw originates in host KVM's per-vCPU MMIO cache, while stale shadow EPT translations permit the guest to access host kernel memory, crossing the guest-to-host virtualization boundary.
C:H - Bypassing kvm_page_track_write() leaves EPT02 translations derived from old EPT12 contents; on affected Linux 6.1.74 this exact stale mapping was demonstrated to provide arbitrary reads of host physical and kernel memory.
I:H - The same stale EPT02 translations were demonstrated to provide arbitrary host-memory writes and host-kernel code execution after emulator_write_emulated() incorrectly routed the tracked EPT12 write through KVM_EXIT_MMIO.
A:H - Arbitrary host-kernel writes and code execution can crash the host and all co-resident VMs; independently, the invalid cache state reaches WARN_ON_ONCE() in kvm_mmu_write_protect_fault(), which panics hardened panic_on_warn hosts.

cna.title: KVM: x86: Use active memslots for the per-vCPU MMIO cache

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bnxt_en: fix DMA mapping length for padded small packets

Stefan Fleischmann reported Intel IOMMU DMA Read faults on BCM57412
NetXtreme-E NICs when transmitting packets on VLAN/macvlan interfaces:

  DMAR: [DMA Read NO_PASID] Request device [18:00.0] fault addr 0xfc499000
        [fault reason 0x06] PTE Read access is not set
  bnxt_en 0000:18:00.0 eno1np0: Abandoning msg {0xb4 0x41a} len: 0 due to firmware status: 0x2000001
  ...
  NETDEV WATCHDOG: eno1np0 (bnxt_en): transmit queue 0 timed out

The fault address (0xfc499000) is on an exact 4KB page boundary,
pointing to a DMA read buffer overrun.

In bnxt_start_xmit(), packets smaller than BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE (52 bytes),
such as 42-byte untagged ARP frames, are padded:

    if (length < BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE) {
        pad = BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE - length;
        if (skb_pad(skb, pad))
            goto tx_kick_pending;
        length = BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE;
    }

    mapping = dma_map_single(&pdev->dev, skb->data, len, DMA_TO_DEVICE);
    ...
    dma_unmap_len_set(tx_buf, len, len);

However, 'len' was initialized earlier to skb_headlen(skb) (e.g. 42 bytes)
and is left unadjusted after padding. Consequently, dma_map_single() and
dma_unmap_len_set() map and track only 42 bytes.

Later, the hardware TX buffer descriptor is programmed with the padded length:

    txbd->tx_bd_len_flags_type =
        cpu_to_le32(((len + pad) << TX_BD_LEN_SHIFT) | flags |
                    TX_BD_FLAGS_PACKET_END);

The NIC DMA engine is thus instructed to read 52 bytes from a region where
only 42 bytes were DMA-mapped. If skb->data ends near the boundary of a 4KB
page (within 'pad' bytes of the next page), the hardware DMA read overruns
into the unmapped adjacent page, triggering an IOMMU fault.

This issue was exposed after commit 447cbe95ebb9 ("vlan: fix skb_under_panic
and races when toggling HW VLAN offload") because reserving extra VLAN
headroom rounded LL_RESERVED_SPACE from 48 up to 64 bytes, shifting skb->data
offsets and potentially causing small frames to land right against page
boundaries.

Fix this by using skb_put_padto(skb, BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE) in
bnxt_start_xmit(), before skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags is sampled,
because padding might linearize the skb.
This ensures skb->len and skb_headlen(skb) reflect the padded size so
that dma_map_single() maps the full buffer and the descriptor length is
consistent. This also removes the temporary 'pad' variable and masking logic.

The padding is done after the SW USO branch, otherwise
bnxt_sw_udp_gso_xmit() would account the padding as UDP payload
and send it in extra segments.

Note that SW USO segments are still not padded: with IPv4, a segment
carrying less than 10 bytes of UDP payload (small gso_size, or a short
last segment) is sent as a frame shorter than BNXT_MIN_PKT_SIZE.
This is a separate issue, left for a followup patch.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A minimal IPv4 ICMP Echo Request follows bnxt_poll→bnxt_rx_pkt→icmp_rcv→icmp_echo; icmp_reply builds a 42-byte reply that reaches the patched bnxt_start_xmit through ip_finish_output2→dev_queue_xmit, including vlan_dev_hard_start_xmit on the reported VLAN setup.
AC:L - A request burst keeps the TX ring nonempty, bypassing the push fast path and repeatedly exercising the 42-to-52-byte mismatch; repeated skb allocations provide the documented 4-KiB boundary placement without a race, second actor, or hardware failure.
PR:N - icmp_rcv and icmp_echo process the Echo Request and invoke icmp_reply without socket credentials, capability checks, or authentication, so the remote sender needs no account or privileges.
UI:N - Receipt of the ICMP Echo Request automatically constructs and transmits the short reply through bnxt_start_xmit; no victim must open a file, run a command, or otherwise act.
S:U - bnxt_start_xmit misprograms the host NIC's TX DMA length, but the IOMMU rejects the overrun rather than being bypassed; no guest, sandbox, or other security authority is crossed.
C:N - skb_pad zero-fills the intended ten padding bytes, while the demonstrated access reaches an unmapped IOVA page and faults; the code provides no path that returns host memory to the routed ICMP peer.
I:N - The erroneous operation is a DMA_TO_DEVICE read of up to ten bytes beyond the mapping; it neither authorizes a NIC write into host memory nor modifies kernel data.
A:H - The 52-byte descriptor read from a 42-byte mapping causes the documented IOMMU fault and NETDEV WATCHDOG TX-queue timeout; bnxt_tx_timeout then schedules bnxt_reset_task to close and reopen the NIC, and repeated requests can continually disrupt all interface traffic.

cna.title: bnxt_en: fix DMA mapping length for padded small packets

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/mlx5e: Prevent stale XSK buffer release on refill retry

When an XDP redirect to an AF_XDP socket fails because its RX ring is
full, the XSK core frees the buffer. During the subsequent batched refill
of a legacy cyclic RQ, mlx5e also releases the WQE's XSK buffer before
allocating a replacement. If that refill succeeds only partially, a WQE
left without a replacement retains its old buffer pointer.

The buffer can meanwhile be allocated to another WQE. A later refill
retry can then free the live buffer through the stale pointer and publish
the same UMEM frame twice.

Mark the WQE as released immediately after the driver-side free. The flag
is already cleared when a replacement buffer is assigned, so refill
retries no longer release stale pointers.

The failure is silent and produces no kernel warning or splat. A
standalone legacy cyclic-RQ zero-copy libxsk reproducer, using 64-byte UDP
traffic offered at 12 Mpps, detected it: stock stopped after 2,854,914
packets in 4.094 seconds, with 4,542 xdp_rx_ring_full events and 64
ownership/double-publication errors. With this change it processed
356,904,225 packets in 30 seconds despite 571,405 xdp_rx_ring_full events,
with no ownership or data errors.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - UDP datagrams reaching mlx5 drive mlx5e_completion_event() -> mlx5e_napi_poll() -> mlx5e_poll_rx_cq()/XDP redirect, then mlx5e_napi_xsk_post() -> mlx5e_post_rx_wqes() -> patched mlx5e_xsk_free_rx_wqe(); sustained routable traffic fills the XSK RX ring and triggers stale release.
AC:L - A sender can sustain small-packet traffic until __xsk_rcv_zc() reports RX-ring-full and mlx5e_xsk_alloc_rx_wqes_batched() refills only part of the missing WQEs; retries are deterministic and require no uncontrolled race or memory layout.
PR:N - The NIC-CQE/NAPI receive path contains no capability or authentication check; xsk_create()'s CAP_NET_RAW check applies to victim-side AF_XDP provisioning, while the remote UDP sender needs no privileges.
UI:N - Once the zero-copy XSK pool and XDP redirect are active, xsk_rcv_zc() failure, mlx5e_napi_xsk_post(), and refill retries occur automatically as packets arrive, without further victim action.
S:U - mlx5e_xsk_free_rx_wqe() corrupts the host kernel's xsk_buff_pool and mlx5 receive state without crossing a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:H - Duplicate xdp_buff_xsk ownership lets repeated successful __xsk_rcv_zc() calls invoke unbounded xp_release(); in unaligned-UMEM mode, free_heads_cnt can write kernel pointers past the flexible free_heads[] array, yielding heap corruption exploitable for arbitrary disclosure.
I:H - The duplicate WQEs can make xp_release() write beyond free_heads[], while xp_get_xskb() later trusts pointers popped through the corrupted count; this supplies out-of-bounds and corrupted-pointer write primitives capable of control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The free_heads[] overflow or a bogus xskb consumed by xp_get_xskb() can oops or panic; additionally, the dma_dev_need_sync refill path can store NULL on allocation failure and have the stale retry pass it to xsk_buff_free().

cna.title: net/mlx5e: Prevent stale XSK buffer release on refill retry

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/mlx5e: Prevent stale XSK buffer release on MPWQE refill retry

With AF_XDP on a striding RQ, mlx5e defers releasing XSK buffers until
an MPWQE is refilled. If XSK allocation then returns -ENOMEM,
actual_wq_head is not advanced and a later NAPI poll retries the same
WQE.

mlx5e_free_rx_mpwqe() leaves each released slot marked as releasable. On
retry it can therefore call xsk_buff_free() again through stale pointers
after the frames have returned to the XSK pool and been reallocated.

Set all skip_release_bitmap bits in the common error path of
mlx5e_xsk_alloc_rx_mpwqe(). This matches mlx5e_alloc_rx_mpwqe(). A
successful allocation already clears the bitmap after replacing every
buffer, so retries become idempotent without changing the success path.

Fault injection forced three consecutive failures for one selected MPWQE.
Both an early allocation failure and a partial 8-of-16-buffer unwind
released the original 16 XSK buffers only once. Each error left a full
bitmap, the following NAPI retry skipped the release, and a later
successful allocation cleared it. A 20-second AF_XDP zero-copy pressure
run exercised 1,575,262 buffer allocation failures without invalid
descriptors, WQE errors, or kernel warnings.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - Routable IP packets received by mlx5 consume the AF_XDP striding RQ through mlx5e_completion_event() -> mlx5e_napi_poll() -> mlx5e_poll_rx_cq(), after which mlx5e_napi_xsk_post() -> mlx5e_post_rx_mpwqes() reaches patched mlx5e_xsk_alloc_rx_mpwqe(); packet pressure exhausts the RX/Fill rings and triggers the stale-buffer retry.
AC:L - A sender can flood the XSK-bound RSS queue until XDP redirect and refill allocation fail, then continue traffic so NAPI retries the unchanged actual_wq_head; no uncontrolled race is needed for mlx5e_free_rx_mpwqe() to release the stale pointer.
PR:N - The receive path beginning at mlx5e_completion_event() performs no authentication or capability check; xsk_create()'s CAP_NET_RAW requirement applies to victim-side AF_XDP provisioning, while the remote IP sender needs no privileges.
UI:N - Once an mlx5 AF_XDP zero-copy pool and XDP program are running, packet receipt, mlx5e_napi_xsk_post(), and the refill retries occur automatically without further victim action.
S:U - The corrupted xsk_buff_pool metadata and mlx5 receive state belong to the host kernel; the bug crosses no VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:H - In unaligned-UMEM mode, duplicate live xdp_buff_xsk ownership lets repeated successful __xsk_rcv_zc() calls make xp_release() write kernel pointers past the pool's flexible free_heads[] array; this heap corruption can be leveraged to disclose arbitrary kernel memory.
I:H - The same xp_release() overflow is an out-of-bounds kernel heap write; subsequent xp_get_xskb() trusts pointers popped from corrupted free_heads[] and initializes through them, supporting arbitrary writes or control-flow corruption.
A:H - Overflowing free_heads[] or later dereferencing a bogus xskb in xp_get_xskb() can oops or panic; even without a crash, duplicate UMEM ownership can prevent mlx5e_xsk_alloc_rx_mpwqe() from restoring WQEs and stop the bound receive queue.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: udp: Create exceptions before socket matching

Currently, when ICMP Fragmentation Needed and Redirect Message packets
are locally delivered and quote a UDP packet, a FIB nexthop exception
(FNHE) is only created if the kernel can match the UDP packet to an
existing socket.

This behavior allows off-path attackers to conduct a side-channel attack
on the FNHE cache in order to discover the ephemeral port used by a
connected UDP socket.

Commit 6457378fe796 ("ipv4: use siphash instead of Jenkins in
fnhe_hashfun()") and commit 67d6d681e15b ("ipv4: make exception cache
less predictible") tried to mitigate such attacks by making it harder
for attackers to discover hash collisions in the FNHE cache and by
randomizing the number of exceptions a hash bucket can hold,
respectively. Unfortunately, both of the mitigations can be bypassed.

Instead, mitigate such attacks by always creating a FNHE, even before
trying to find a matching socket. Do that by calling ipv4_update_pmtu()
and ipv4_redirect(), the helpers used when the quoted packet did not
originate from a socket.

This means that guesses (right or wrong) from an off-path attacker will
always result in a FNHE being created or updated in the cache that the
attacker can observe.

Pass an oif of 0, in a similar fashion to icmp_err(). This is also the
oif used by the socket path for sockets that are not bound to a device.

Note that this does not allow attackers to create FNHEs that they could
not create before, as both helpers can already be reached with little to
no validation. For example, by sending an ICMP error that quotes an ICMP
Echo Reply or one that quotes a UDP source port that matches a wildcard
socket.

Also note that in the good case (matched socket) the above scheme comes
at the cost of an extra route lookup, as the no socket helpers perform
their own lookup before the one performed by ipv4_sk_update_pmtu() /
ipv4_sk_redirect(). When the two resolve to different nexthops, it also
results in two exceptions being created for the same destination IP. One
in the FNHE cache of the nexthop resolved by the no socket helpers and
another in the FNHE cache of the nexthop used by the socket.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A remote IPv4 ICMP Fragmentation Needed or Redirect message carries the attacker-controlled inner IPv4/UDP quote through ip_rcv(), icmp_rcv(), icmp_socket_deliver(), and udp_err(), where its guessed four-tuple is matched.
AC:H - Exploiting a connected socket requires turning fnhe_hashfun() bucket occupancy and update_or_create_fnhe() eviction into an oracle while the UDP tuple remains live; keyed hashing, randomized bucket depth, cache noise, and the short DNS response window are conditions the attacker cannot fully determine, although the mitigations can be bypassed.
PR:N - icmp_rcv() checks packet structure, checksum, and policy but has no authentication or capability gate; icmp_unreach() passes a valid Fragmentation Needed quote to udp_err() without verifying that its sender is an on-path router.
UI:N - The attacker can induce a resolver's connected UDP socket with a DNS query and then send the ICMP probes and cache-verification traffic; no victim user action is required.
S:U - The FNHE oracle in udp_err() compromises networking and application data governed by the same host security authority; it does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary.
C:H - The __udp4_lib_lookup() result controls whether ipv4_sk_update_pmtu() or ipv4_sk_redirect() leaves an observable FNHE, disclosing the complete ephemeral source port. On a recursive DNS resolver, removing that entropy enables cache poisoning and redirection of client traffic, permitting broad disclosure.
I:H - After learning the port, the same attacker can forge UDP DNS replies and brute-force the remaining transaction ID; an accepted reply can poison the resolver cache and map chosen names to attacker-controlled addresses.
A:N - The fixed defect is the match-dependent FNHE oracle, not memory corruption or a crash. update_or_create_fnhe() already accepts other minimally validated ICMP cases, and the fix deliberately preserves exception creation, so route-cache manipulation is not an availability impact removed by this patch.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cipso: adjust cached option offsets when removing CIPSO

cipso_v4_skbuff_delattr() removes the CIPSO bytes but does not adjust
cached offsets for options that follow them.

For example, with a valid 10-byte CIPSO option followed by a seven-byte
RR option, parsing records rr at offset 30.  Removing CIPSO moves RR to
offset 20, while the cached offset remains 30.  Consumers such as
ip_forward_options() and __ip_options_echo() then access the wrong bytes;
the latter may interpret packet data as the option length and copy it into
fixed-size option storage.

Mirror cipso_v4_delopt() and subtract cipso_len from the srr, rr, ts and
router_alert offsets when they follow CIPSO.  cipso_len is the distance
the first memmove() shifts those options.  The later header move and
network-header reset relocate the bytes and their offset base together.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A remote peer can send an IPv4 datagram containing valid CIPSO followed by RR/TS; ip_rcv()->ip_rcv_options() caches their wire offsets, then selinux_ip_forward()->netlbl_skbuff_setattr()->cipso_v4_skbuff_delattr() removes CIPSO without rebasing them.
AC:H - The strongest path requires a CONFIG_NETLABEL/SELinux forwarding gateway with network_peer_controls, a recognized CIPSO DOI, an UNLABELED egress mapping, and a later FORWARD REJECT invoking nf_send_unreach(); these non-default conditions are outside the sender's control.
PR:N - __ip_options_compile() applies CAP_NET_RAW only when skb is NULL; received packets undergo cipso_v4_validate() and SELinux label-policy checks, but require no peer authentication, victim credentials, or target-side privileges.
UI:N - After the datagram arrives, ip_rcv(), SELinux FORWARD relabeling, and nf_send_unreach()->__ip_options_echo() execute entirely in kernel packet handling without any victim action.
S:U - The overwrite occurs in __ip_options_echo()'s in-kernel reply-option storage and can compromise the same host kernel; it crosses no VM, IOMMU, or separate security-authority boundary.
C:H - With stale opt->rr pointing into payload, __ip_options_echo() takes an attacker-chosen length and source bytes and copies up to 255 bytes into 40-byte replyopts.opt.__data; control-flow compromise from this stack overwrite can expose arbitrary kernel memory.
I:H - The memcpy() can place 255 attacker-controlled payload bytes into the 40-byte stack destination, crossing the stack canary and saved return address in the demonstrated x86-64 layout and enabling kernel control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The 255-byte __ip_options_echo() stack overwrite triggers KASAN or the stack canary and can panic the kernel; the packet-processing path can be invoked repeatedly with crafted IPv4 datagrams.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wireguard: noise: reject response consumption after intermediate initiation

Two threads begin processing the identical response message, received
twice. The first thread, A, runs. While it's running, the second one,
B, gets partway through, and during that slow calculation, or even while
blocking on down_write(), A completes and then also a handshake
initiation that's already been queued up runs in thread C, which itself
takes that same down_write(). The handshake initiation creation
succeeds, and sets the state back to waiting-for-response, and calls
up_write(), at which point thread B resumes, because either its finished
its calculations or was finally allowed to acquire down_write(). Thread
B then copies the state back to the peer, and begins a new session,
using that state, which is the same session as the one made in thread A.

Thread A			Thread B			Thread C

down_read()
 sA = handshake->state
 memcpy(cA, handshake->crypto)
up_read()
if (sA != 1)
 goto fail
slow_crypto(cA)
				down_read()
				 sB = handshake->state
				 memcpy(cB, handshake->crypto)
				up_read()
				if (sB != 1)
				 goto fail
				slow_crypto(cB)
down_write()
 if (sA != handshake->state)
  goto fail
 memcpy(handshake->crypto, cA)
 handshake->state = 2
up_write()
down_write()
 if (handshake->state != 2)
  goto fail
 derive_session(handshake->crypto)
up_write()
								down_write()
								 slow_crypto(handshake->crypto)
								 handshake->state = 1
								up_write()
				down_write()
				 if (sB != handshake->state)
				   goto fail
				 memcpy(handshake->crypto, cB)
				 handshake->state = 2
				up_write()
				down_write()
				 if (handshake->state != 2)
				  goto fail
				 derive_session(handshake->crypto)
				up_write()

This seems basically impossible to hit in a meaningful way in practice,
but ensure that it absolutely cannot happen by comparing the ephemeral
private key that's on the stack with the latest one that the peer's
handshake state has.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - An IPv4/IPv6 UDP MESSAGE_HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE follows wg_receive() -> wg_packet_receive() -> wg_packet_handshake_receive_worker() -> wg_receive_handshake_packet() -> patched wg_noise_handshake_consume_response(); replayed response bytes drive the race over a routable WireGuard endpoint.
AC:H - Success requires responses A and B to snapshot the same initiation while a jittered retransmission has queued C, followed by the exact A-to-C-to-B write-lock ordering. The random REKEY_TIMEOUT jitter and host worker scheduling are not controlled by the attacker.
PR:N - A byte-identical captured response passes wg_cookie_validate_packet() and the encrypted_nothing check in message_decrypt() when replayed, so an on-path attacker need not possess a configured peer's private or preshared key.
UI:N - The attacker delays and duplicates the UDP response, while wg_expired_retransmit_handshake() automatically queues the intermediate initiation; no victim action is required during exploitation.
S:U - The duplicate sessions remain within the same peer's noise_keypairs and compromise traffic handled by that WireGuard device under the same kernel security authority; no VM, IOMMU, or other authority boundary is crossed.
C:H - Both calls to wg_noise_handshake_begin_session() run derive_keys() on the same chaining_key, while each keypair_create() starts sending_counter at zero. Reusing ChaCha20 keys and nonces across transport packets can expose substantial tunnel plaintext.
I:H - encrypt_packet() authenticates transport ciphertext with ChaCha20-Poly1305 using the duplicated key and reset counter as its nonce. Reusing that Poly1305 one-time key permits an on-path attacker to construct forged authenticated tunnel packets for colliding counters.
A:L - The reset sending_counter repeats counters already used by the first session, so the peer's counter_validate() replay window discards colliding packets until the new counter catches up or a rekey occurs. This interrupts tunnel traffic but does not corrupt memory or crash the kernel.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

strparser: make sure __strp_recv isn't running before tearing down the parser

The comment above strp_done() claims that if strp is stopped,
strp_recv will no longer be called. That's only true if the caller has
a mechanism (eg locking) to guarantee that strp_recv() calls that
started before strp_stop() have completed by the time we call
strp_done().

This adds a dummy lock_sock/release_sock pair to guarantee that any
in-flight strp_recv() (which runs under either bh_lock_sock or
lock_sock, depending if it's called from ->sk_data_ready or strp_work)
has completed.

Only espintcp can be affected by this race condition, but this patch
makes sure no future user of strp can have the bug.

This could crash on strp->sk ("general mode" of strp), but this mode
has been here for 9 years and has never been used. It'll be gone soon,
no point worrying about it.

Switch the stopped/paused/etc bits to u8's to avoid races between
strp_stop() and strp_pause/unpause().

A reproducer has been published and turns the possible UAF into an
exploit [1].

scenarios.value:
AV:L - An unprivileged local process can attach "espintcp" with setsockopt(TCP_ULP), then use a loopback peer to drive espintcp_data_ready()->strp_data_ready()->__strp_recv() while close() reaches espintcp_close()->strp_done(); a network peer alone cannot initiate the required local teardown.
AC:L - The same process controls both race sides: it sets a finite SO_RCVTIMEO, sends complete keepalives plus a partial header that makes espintcp_parse() return 0 and strp_start_timer() rearm after strp_done() cancels, and concurrently closes the target socket. The race is repeatable and publicly exploited.
PR:L - __sys_setsockopt()->tcp_setsockopt()->tcp_set_ulp()->espintcp_init_sk() contains no capability or authentication check for an already registered "espintcp" ULP. An ordinary local user can create the TCP pair, set the timeout, attach the ULP, and close it.
UI:N - The attacking process performs the socket creation, TCP_ULP attachment, traffic generation, close, and heap reclaim itself; no action by another user is required.
S:U - The reclaimed espintcp_ctx and its msg_timer_work execute within the host kernel reached by the attacking local process; this is a conventional local kernel privilege escalation and crosses no VM, IOMMU, or separate security authority.
C:H - The freed espintcp_ctx can be reclaimed with a controlled user_key_payload, including msg_timer_work.timer.function and callback operands. The resulting kernel callback control and root execution permit access to arbitrary protected memory.
I:H - The controlled timer.function and RDI-relative operands let the demonstrated iocg_flush_stat_upward gadget perform a chosen delta write to modprobe_path, producing root code execution.
A:H - If the freed msg_timer_work is not coherently reclaimed, timer expiry consumes stale work_struct fields or calls an invalid timer.function, causing a kernel fault or panic; the published exploit also documents a crash-only variant.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tipc: destroy topsrv workqueues before closing connections

tipc_topsrv_stop() closed subscriber connections while the topology
server's send and receive workqueues were still running. Socket
callbacks and subscription events could then queue more work, and
in-flight send/recv work could drop the last connection reference
during the conn_idr walk.

That race produced several teardown failures: refcount_t addition on
0 from conn_get() on a connection whose release was blocked on
idr_lock, a subsequent use-after-free in tipc_conn_close(),
queue_work() on an already destroyed workqueue from the listener
data-ready callback, and an RCU stall in tipc_topsrv_exit_net()
while the walk spun under idr_lock.

Clear srv->listener under idr_lock so it acts as a shutdown flag,
skip queue_work() once it is NULL, destroy the workqueues to flush
in-flight work, and only then close the remaining connections.
Refuse tipc_conn_lookup() after that flag is cleared, and drop
idr_lock when the teardown walk finds no connection, so an
in-flight subscription event cannot pin idr_in_use while the
walk holds the lock.

v3 supersedes the narrower in-thread diff Tung Quang Nguyen
posted on 2026-09-23. It keeps his teardown order and adds the
lookup refusal and the empty-idr unlock.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER|CLONE_NEWNET)` creates the per-net TIPC server; local `socket(AF_TIPC)`, `connect(TIPC_TOP_SRV)`, and `send()` churn followed by exit drives `cleanup_net()` -> `tipc_topsrv_exit_net()` -> patched `tipc_topsrv_stop()`. No remote message can cause the required namespace teardown.
AC:L - The attacker controls both sides of the race: worker threads repeatedly create and close topology subscriptions while their process exits the network namespace, racing `rwork`/`swork` and socket callbacks against `tipc_topsrv_stop()`. No victim or hardware state is required.
PR:L - `tipc_sk_create()`, `tipc_connect()`, and `tipc_conn_rcv_sub()` have no capability or authentication gate; an ordinary user can obtain the `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` needed for `CLONE_NEWNET` inside a new user namespace. No init-namespace privilege is required.
UI:N - The attacker creates the namespaces, opens and floods `TIPC_TOP_SRV` connections, closes them, and exits to start `cleanup_net()` without any victim action.
S:U - The freed `tipc_conn` and workqueue objects belong to the host kernel, and exploitation of `tipc_topsrv_stop()` affects that same kernel authority without crossing a VM, IOMMU, or other security boundary.
C:H - `tipc_conn_kref_release()` frees `con` while teardown retains its address; `tipc_conn_close()` then reads `con->sock->sk` and follows reclaimed subscription and socket pointers. Reclaiming this object permits attacker-controlled pointer dereferences usable as kernel-memory read primitives.
I:H - After the free, `tipc_conn_close()` modifies reclaimed `con->flags`, writes through `sk->sk_user_data`, processes reclaimed subscription lists, and calls `kernel_sock_shutdown()` through `con->sock->ops`. These provide memory-write and control-flow primitives.
A:H - The reported race produced a page fault in `tipc_conn_close()`, `queue_work()` on a destroyed receive workqueue, and an RCU stall in `tipc_topsrv_exit_net()`; these paths can oops, panic, or wedge the system.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tipc: hold a reference to nodes found by link name

tipc_node_find_by_name() returns a node after dropping its RCU read lock
without taking a reference.  The LINK_SET, LINK_GET and LINK_RESET_STATS
handlers then lock and access the node, racing with timer-driven cleanup of
a down peer.  Generic netlink serialization does not exclude the node
timer.

The following interleaving can leave a handler using a freed node:

  CPU 0: find the node under RCU and release the node read lock
  CPU 1: tipc_node_timeout() clears the links and unlinks the down node
  CPU 1: drop the list and timer references, queuing tipc_node_free()
  CPU 0: leave the RCU read-side critical section
  CPU 1: complete the grace period and free the node
  CPU 0: acquire the node lock through the stale pointer

LINK_SET also uses the node's media address after releasing the node lock,
when passing queued packets to tipc_bearer_xmit().

KASAN on v7.3-rc5 reported:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in _raw_read_lock_bh
  Write of size 4 at addr ffff88807e06f008 by task poc/92
  Call Trace:
   _raw_read_lock_bh                 kernel/locking/spinlock.c:287
   tipc_nl_node_set_link             net/tipc/node.c:2475
   genl_family_rcv_msg_doit          net/netlink/genetlink.c:1114
   genl_rcv_msg                      net/netlink/genetlink.c:1209
   netlink_rcv_skb                   net/netlink/af_netlink.c:2575

  Allocated by task 0:
   tipc_node_create                  net/tipc/node.c:539
   tipc_node_check_dest              net/tipc/node.c:1196
   tipc_disc_rcv                     net/tipc/discover.c:252

  Freed by task 92:
   kfree                             mm/slub.c:6801
   rcu_core                          kernel/rcu/tree.c:2919

  Last potentially related work creation:
   __call_rcu_common.constprop.0     kernel/rcu/tree.c:3181
   tipc_node_timeout                 net/tipc/node.c:814

Acquire a reference to the selected node with kref_get_unless_zero() before
leaving RCU, returning NULL if the node has already been released.  Release
that reference on every caller exit after the last node access, including
transmission in LINK_SET.  Keep the existing link lookup order and locking
so concurrent link removal still takes the existing error paths.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The attacker-controlled selector is TIPC_NLA_LINK_NAME in a local NETLINK_GENERIC TIPC_NL_LINK_GET request, dispatched to tipc_nl_node_get_link() and patched tipc_node_find_by_name(). Remote packets can create or down the peer but cannot invoke this handler, so one remote actor cannot trigger the UAF.
AC:L - The same local attacker can create TIPC peers in user/network namespaces, stop one so node_lost_contact() sets delete_at, and flood LINK_GET while tipc_node_timeout() performs cleanup. Both sides of this repeatable race are attacker-controlled, and the submitted PoC reached the KASAN UAF.
PR:L - TIPC_NL_LINK_GET is registered without an administrative permission flag and reaches tipc_nl_node_get_link() for any local netlink caller. Setup mutators use GENL_UNS_ADMIN_PERM and the family has netnsok=true, allowing an unprivileged user to obtain the necessary namespace-local rights.
UI:N - The attacker can create and stop its own TIPC peer and issue the racing TIPC_NL_LINK_GET requests without any victim action.
S:U - The stale pointer from tipc_node_find_by_name() corrupts host-kernel tipc_node and tipc_link slab objects; no VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary is crossed.
C:H - TIPC_NL_LINK_GET follows a reclaimed node->links[bearer_id].link into __tipc_nl_add_link(), which copies link names, properties, and statistics into the attacker's netlink reply. Heap grooming can therefore turn the stale node into an arbitrary kernel-read primitive.
I:H - _raw_read_lock_bh() already performs the reported four-byte write to freed node->lock. With a reclaimed links pointer, TIPC_NL_LINK_RESET_STATS reaches tipc_link_reset_stats(), whose memset() provides an attacker-directed kernel write suitable for further corruption or control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The observed slab use-after-free occurs while tipc_nl_node_set_link() locks the freed node; corrupted lock state or the subsequent stale node/link dereferences can cause a kernel oops or panic.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

fsverity: RCU-delay the freeing of struct fsverity_info

__fsverity_get_info() calls rhashtable_lookup_fast(), which just uses
rcu_read_lock() and doesn't directly synchronize with
fsverity_remove_info().

For the same inode this isn't a problem: its fsverity_info is removed
only at inode eviction time or upon failure to enable verity, when the
inode no longer needs its fsverity_info and it will no longer be
accessed via that inode.

However, this is broken and can cause a use-after-free for concurrent
__fsverity_get_info() for *different* inodes.  Those rely on following
fsverity_info::rhash_head in the rhashtable under rcu_read_lock() only.
They also use fsverity_info::inode to do the key comparison.

Fix this by RCU-delaying the freeing of 'struct fsverity_info' after
it's been removed from the rhashtable.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - `ioctl(FS_IOC_MEASURE_VERITY)` reaches `fsverity_ioctl_measure()` and `fsverity_get_info()`, while `unlinkat()`/`close()` of another fs-verity file reaches `clear_inode()`, `fsverity_cleanup_inode()`, and patched `fsverity_remove_info()`; these are local syscall paths, not wire data.
AC:L - An attacker can enable many owned files to populate colliding rhashtable chains, then loop measurements of one inode while concurrently unlinking and closing the others; the attacker controls both lookup and freeing and can repeat the race.
PR:L - `fsverity_ioctl_enable()` checks only `file_permission(filp, MAY_WRITE)`, `FMODE_READ`, and a writable mount, with no capability check; lookup and eviction require only ordinary access to attacker-owned files on btrfs or verity-enabled ext4/f2fs.
UI:N - The attacker can create, enable, measure, unlink, and close all participating files using their own processes, without another user mounting media or taking any action.
S:U - The dangling object belongs to the host kernel's `fsverity_info_hash` and `fsverity_info_cachep`; corrupting it affects the same kernel security authority and crosses no VM, IOMMU, or hypervisor boundary.
C:H - `fsverity_remove_info()` frees the slab while `__rhashtable_lookup()` still reads `inode` and `rhash_head.next`; after cache reuse, a misdirected lookup is consumed by `fsverity_ioctl_measure()`, which dereferences `tree_params` and copies `file_digest` to userspace.
I:H - File-read consumers pass the lookup result to `fsverity_verify_blocks()`, whose `clear_bit()` and `set_bit()` write through `vi->hash_block_verified`; attacker-groomed reuse of the freed object can therefore turn the UAF into arbitrary kernel-memory corruption.
A:H - `kmem_cache_free()` permits allocator metadata to replace the freed `rhash_head.next` while the rhashtable loop still follows `pos->next`, which can oops or panic the kernel; repeated measure-and-evict cycles can retrigger it.

cna.title: fsverity: RCU-delay the freeing of struct fsverity_info

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

gpio: mpsse: fix race when arming the IRQ poll worker

gpio_mpsse_irq_enable() arms the poll worker before publishing it:
schedule_work() runs before the worker is added to priv->workers. If
gpio_mpsse_disconnect() walks the list in that window it misses the
worker, and once disconnect returns, the USB core frees mpsse_priv
while the orphaned gpio_mpsse_poll() work keeps accessing it, causing
a use-after-free.

Fix this by publishing and arming the worker in one irq_spin
critical section. Teardown walks the same list under irq_spin, so a
worker found on the list is guaranteed to be armed, and
cancel_work_sync() handles it whether it is queued or running.

A worker armed after the disconnect walk would still be missed, so
also set a new priv->dying flag under irq_spin before the teardown
walk, and check it in the same critical section, freeing it via
kfree_rcu() instead when the device is going away, since kfree()
would be called with the IRQ core's raw spinlock held and may sleep
on PREEMPT_RT. schedule_work() is safe to call with irq_spin held,
and the next probe gets a fresh mpsse_priv, so the flag never needs
to be cleared.

This issue was found by an in-house static analysis tool.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A local process can race GPIO_V2_GET_LINE_IOCTL -> linereq_create() -> edge_detector_setup() -> request_threaded_irq() -> gpio_mpsse_irq_enable() against USBDEVFS_IOCTL/USBDEVFS_DISCONNECT -> usb_driver_release_interface() -> gpio_mpsse_disconnect(); no network input reaches the bug.
AC:L - The attacker can issue the GPIO line-event request and USBFS unbind concurrently and repeat after rebinding; both sides of the schedule_work()-before-list_add() window are attacker-controlled.
PR:L - Neither gpio_ioctl() nor the USBDEVFS_DISCONNECT path performs a capability check; the process only needs non-root DAC/ACL access to /dev/gpiochipN and writable access to the matching /dev/bus/usb node.
UI:N - The same process submits the line-event and USB disconnect ioctls that create the race, so no action by another user is required.
S:U - The freed mpsse_priv and orphaned gpio_mpsse_poll() worker are both in the host kernel; the path crosses no VM, IOMMU, or other security authority.
C:H - gpio_mpsse_poll() continues through attacker-reclaimable mpsse_priv fields, including GPIO, IRQ-domain, USB-buffer, and interface pointers; the resulting UAF and write primitive can yield kernel code execution and unrestricted reads.
I:H - gpio_mpsse_poll() locks and traverses priv->workers after priv is freed; reclaiming that allocation lets controlled list pointers reach list_del(), providing attacker-directed kernel writes and control-flow corruption.
A:H - The orphaned gpio_mpsse_poll() can access freed mutex, spinlock, and list state, or use the NULL/stale priv->intf in MPSSE I/O, causing an oops or kernel panic.

cna.title: gpio: mpsse: fix race when arming the IRQ poll worker

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

gve: fix XSK buffer leak on error descriptor

When the error bit is set in the RX completion descriptor, the buf_state
and its attached buffer should be freed. In the case of AF_XDP ZC, the
XSK buffer was not freed, leading to a leak.

This issue was caught by LLM.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A malformed Ethernet/IP packet received by gVNIC produces a DQO completion whose rx_error field denotes an invalid packet; gve_intr_dqo() schedules gve_napi_poll_dqo(), which reaches the patched gve_rx_dqo() through gve_rx_poll_dqo().
AC:L - With a DQO-RDA AF_XDP zero-copy queue active, the sender can repeatedly transmit packets classified by the device as invalid; gve_rx_dqo() then deterministically takes the rx_error branch without a race or memory-layout dependency.
PR:N - The gve_rx_dqo() receive path performs no authentication or capability check; xsk_create()'s CAP_NET_RAW check and XDP attachment are victim-side service provisioning, while the remote sender needs only packet access.
UI:N - After gve_reg_xsk_pool() activates the pool, gve_intr_dqo() and NAPI process each error completion automatically without any victim action.
S:U - The leak affects the guest kernel's own GVE XSK pool and DQO receive queue; it neither bypasses an IOMMU nor crosses the guest/hypervisor boundary.
C:N - The lost xdp_buff_xsk remains allocated but unreturned; the branch performs no out-of-bounds read or data return, and gve_alloc_buf_state() clears the stale pointer before reusing the state.
I:N - In the vulnerable XSK case, gve_free_buffer() releases only page-pool state and the buf_state while leaving the XSK object allocated, causing resource loss without a dangling access, memory corruption, or unauthorized modification.
A:H - Each error completion omits xsk_buff_free()/xp_free(), removing one frame from the fixed XSK pool; repetition makes xsk_buff_alloc() fail in gve_alloc_buffer(), prevents RX-buffer reposting, and can stop the bound receive queue until the pool or service is reset.

cna.title: gve: fix XSK buffer leak on error descriptor

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/net: populate CONNECT filter fields for 24-byte sockaddr_in6

io_connect_bpf_populate() fills connect.port and connect.v6_addr for
AF_INET6 only when addr_len >= sizeof(struct sockaddr_in6), i.e. 28
bytes.

The IPv6 connect paths accept SIN6_LEN_RFC2133 (24 bytes), which
already holds sin6_port and sin6_addr. io_connect() passes addr_len to
the socket layer unchanged.

At addr_len 24 the filter sees family AF_INET6 with port and address
zero, while the kernel connects to the real destination. A filter that
denies an IPv6 port or address is bypassed. Denying connect.port == P
rejects [::1]:P with -EACCES at addr_len 28 but connects at addr_len 24.

Use SIN6_LEN_RFC2133 as the threshold. sin6_scope_id stays zero when
absent.

The threshold mismatch was found by an AI coding assistant (Claude Code)
comparing this hook against the net/ipv6 length checks on my
instructions; it also drafted the reproducer and this patch. I verified
the bypass and the fix in a VM on 7.3-rc6 and that 7.2 has the same
code.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - An attacker reaches the patched io_connect_bpf_populate() by locally submitting IORING_OP_CONNECT through io_uring_enter(), with sqe->addr2 supplying the malicious 24-byte length. No network packet carries the value creating the mismatch.
AC:L - Against a CONNECT filter denying an IPv6 port or address, addr2=24 deterministically makes io_connect_bpf_populate() expose zero port/address while tcp_v6_connect() accepts and uses the real fields; no race or uncontrolled condition is involved.
PR:L - No capability check exists in io_uring_enter(), io_connect_prep(), or io_connect(), and AF_INET6 SOCK_STREAM creation avoids inet6_create()'s CAP_NET_RAW check. An ordinary confined process with access to the filtered ring can trigger the bypass.
UI:N - The confined process prepares and submits the 24-byte sockaddr itself, and io_connect_prep() copies it during io_uring_enter(); no other user must mount, open, approve, or otherwise act.
S:C - The false port/address view escapes the io_uring BPF CONNECT sandbox: __io_uring_run_bpf_filters() allows an operation that an inherited or ring-level filter intended to deny, reaching network resources outside that policy scope.
C:H - After the filter sees :: and port 0, tcp_v6_connect() uses sin6_addr and sin6_port from the same 24 bytes; the confined process can establish a full socket and read responses from IPv6 services the CONNECT filter explicitly made inaccessible.
I:H - tcp_v6_connect() stores the hidden destination in sk_v6_daddr and inet_dport and establishes the denied socket, enabling arbitrary application data and requests to be sent to IPv6 services and ports prohibited by the sandbox policy.
A:N - The bug only substitutes zero values in the filter context; move_addr_to_kernel() safely copies 24 bytes and the IPv6 socket layer accepts that size. It introduces no corruption, out-of-bounds access, oops, hang, or resource exhaustion.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/smc: protect clcsock lifetime in smc_getname

smc_getname() dereferences smc->clcsock without holding
clcsock_release_lock. Link-group termination can release the CLC socket
through smc_close_active_abort() while the SMC socket is still open,
for example after shutdown(SHUT_WR).

A getsockname() caller can load smc->clcsock, then the termination worker
can clear the pointer and call sock_release() before the caller accesses
clcsock->ops or invokes getname(). This causes a use-after-free; if the
worker clears the pointer before the load, it causes a NULL dereference.
The syscall's file reference keeps the SMC socket alive but does not
prevent asynchronous release of its CLC socket.

KASAN reported the following with test-only timing instrumentation:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in smc_getname+0x19e/0x1b0
  Read of size 8 at addr ffff888109abb4e0 by task poc/103
  Call Trace:
   smc_getname+0x19e/0x1b0
   do_getsockname+0xe5/0x170
   __sys_getsockname+0x8c/0x100

  Allocated by task 95:
   sock_alloc_inode+0x1e/0x280
   sock_alloc+0x3d/0x240
   __sock_create+0x7e/0x430
   smc_create+0x121/0x240

  Freed by task 0:
   kmem_cache_free+0xcc/0x340
   rcu_core+0x50a/0x1850

  Last potentially related work creation:
   evict+0x446/0x6c0
   smc_clcsock_release+0xa8/0xd0
   smc_close_active_abort+0x26a/0x3a0
   __smc_lgr_terminate.part.0+0x137/0x2e0

Hold clcsock_release_lock across the pointer check and the getname()
callback to serialize with smc_clcsock_release(). Return -EBADF if the
CLC socket has already been released, preserving the existing peer
state check and the callback's return value otherwise.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - getsockname(2) on an attacker-owned SMC fd follows __sys_getsockname()->do_getsockname()->smc_getname(), whose unlocked clcsock dereference is the fault; no SMC/TCP message invokes smc_getname(), so a remote peer alone cannot trigger it.
AC:L - After shutdown(SHUT_WR) moves the socket to SMC_PEERCLOSEWAIT1, the attacker can loop getsockname() while its SMC peer sends LLC DELETE LINK ALL, driving __smc_lgr_terminate()->smc_close_active_abort()->smc_clcsock_release(); both race sides are attacker-controlled.
PR:L - smc_create() accepts SOCK_STREAM with SMCPROTO_SMC or SMCPROTO_SMC6 without capable() or ns_capable(), while shutdown() and getsockname() require only the socket fd; an ordinary local user can execute the complete path.
UI:N - The attacker creates and connects the SMC socket, calls shutdown(SHUT_WR), and races getsockname() against termination without requiring another user to mount, open, or approve anything.
S:U - smc_getname() and the freed CLC socket execute within the same host kernel security authority; this path crosses no guest-host, IOMMU, or other separately governed boundary.
C:H - The stale struct socket contains both ops and sk; after sock_inode_cache reuse, the indirect getname callback can consume attacker-groomed recycled socket state and return data to userspace, giving the UAF a kernel-memory disclosure primitive.
I:H - The freed struct socket supplies the indirect ops->getname target and its sk operand; reclaiming it with attacker-created sockets permits callback/operand confusion and mutable kernel-socket access, supporting control-flow or write-oriented exploitation.
A:H - If smc_clcsock_release() clears the pointer first, smc_getname() dereferences NULL; if freeing follows the caller's load, KASAN confirms a slab use-after-free. Either path can produce a kernel oops or panic.

cna.title: net/smc: protect clcsock lifetime in smc_getname

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: skbuff: don't leave stale bytes in skb_copy_and_csum_bits()

When skb_copy_and_csum_bits() reaches unreadable frags it returns 0
after copying only the linear part, and the rest of the caller's buffer
is left as it was.  The callers copy into a buffer that is about to go
out on the wire: an ICMP error quoting the offending packet, or a
driver's TX bounce buffer in skb_copy_and_csum_dev().  Neither buffer
is zeroed beforehand, so whatever was in memory there gets sent.

Zero the part of the buffer we didn't fill.  The checksum usually
won't match the data any more, so the receiver will usually drop the
packet, but either way it no longer carries anything it shouldn't.
Only zero for a positive @len, a negative one from a broken caller must
not turn into a huge memset().

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A remote peer can send an IPv4/TCP segment with an IPOPT_RR length of 2 and payload into a devmem RX flow; ip_rcv() -> ip_rcv_finish_core() -> ip_rcv_options() -> icmp_send() -> icmp_glue_bits() reaches the patched skb_copy_and_csum_bits() while constructing ICMP_PARAMETERPROB.
AC:L - With documented devmem header splitting and RX-queue binding active, the peer controls the invalid option and payload length, so the unreadable-fragment return and stale transmission occur deterministically; no race or uncontrollable condition is required.
PR:N - ip_options_compile() emits ICMP_PARAMETERPROB before tcp_v4_rcv() performs TCP-state processing or any application authentication; neither this path nor skb_copy_and_csum_bits() checks a target credential or capability.
UI:N - The peer's malformed segment alone drives ip_rcv_options() and the ICMP reply; an already-active devmem flow is service configuration, and no victim must respond, open data, or perform another action.
S:U - The uninitialized ICMP transmit buffer and the prior skb-head contents it exposes are both managed by the same host kernel; the flaw crosses no VM, IOMMU, or sandbox security authority.
C:H - skb_copy_and_csum_bits() copies only the linear headers and can leave roughly 500 bytes of a 548-byte IPv4 ICMP quote stale in an unzeroed alloc_skb() buffer; repeatable replies transmit prior skb-head contents, supporting substantial remote data harvesting.
I:N - skb_copy_and_csum_bits() writes the copied header within the allocated destination and merely leaves its tail untouched; there is no out-of-bounds write, attacker-controlled kernel modification, or persistent state corruption.
A:N - The vulnerable branch returns zero without faulting, looping, or exhausting resources; its incorrect checksum may cause the receiver to drop the ICMP reply, but it does not crash or degrade the target kernel.

cna.title: net: skbuff: don't leave stale bytes in skb_copy_and_csum_bits()

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

riscv: entry: gate shadow call stack reload on sstatus.SPP, not tp

Under CONFIG_SHADOW_CALL_STACK, handle_exception() reloads the kernel
shadow call stack pointer (gp) only when the trap came from userspace.
It made that decision with scs_load_current_if_task_changed, which
compares the trap-time tp (read back from sscratch into s5) against the
current tp:

	beq	\prev, tp, _skip_scs
	scs_load_current
_skip_scs:

tp is a user-writable register.  A user task that sets tp to the
linear-map address of its own task_struct (&current) before trapping
makes the comparison succeed (can achieve by brute force with KASLR
enable under our test), so the kernel skips scs_load_current and
keeps running with the gp that userspace left in place.  Under
CONFIG_SHADOW_CALL_STACK gp is the shadow call stack pointer and
load_global_pointer is a no-op, so the compiler-emitted
"sd ra, -8(gp)" / "ld ra, -8(gp)" in every non-leaf function then write
to, and return through, an attacker-controlled address -- an
unprivileged kernel arbitrary-write and control-flow-hijack primitive.
The poisoned gp is saved to task_struct.scs_sp on return, so the reload
is skipped on every subsequent entry as well.

Decide "came from userspace" from the hardware sstatus.SPP bit (already
in s1 at this point) instead of from tp, mirroring the check that
ret_from_exception already uses a few instructions later.  SPP is
written by hardware on trap entry and cannot be forged from U-mode.
Legitimate behaviour is unchanged: user entries (SPP=0) reload the task
shadow call stack, nested kernel entries (SPP=1) skip it.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A U-mode RISC-V task controls the ordinary tp/gp registers and executes ecall; stvec enters handle_exception(), whose scs_load_current_if_task_changed macro consumes those values before do_trap_ecall_u. No wire or physical device carries the causal data.
AC:L - On a CONFIG_SHADOW_CALL_STACK kernel, wrong tp guesses simply invoke scs_load_current, while a match to &current skips it; the fix explicitly reports successfully brute-forcing that match with KASLR enabled. No race or victim-controlled state is required.
PR:L - The vulnerable comparison occurs in handle_exception() before do_trap_ecall_u reaches syscall_enter_from_user_mode_randomize_stack() or any syscall permission check; U-mode may write tp/gp and execute ecall without capabilities.
UI:N - After the attacker's own ecall poisons gp, ret_from_exception saves it into task_struct.scs_sp; no victim must open, mount, approve, or race anything.
S:U - The forged SCS pointer pivots execution inside the same Linux kernel that handles the caller's ecall; the path crosses no KVM guest-host or IOMMU security authority.
C:H - Because load_global_pointer is a no-op, attacker-selected gp controls compiler SCS loads such as ld ra,-8(gp); the resulting supervisor-mode control-flow hijack permits arbitrary kernel-memory disclosure.
I:H - Compiler SCS stores such as sd ra,-8(gp) write through the attacker-selected gp to a chosen kernel address, and the corresponding return-address control enables arbitrary kernel code execution.
A:H - The attacker can direct the SCS store/load at invalid or critical kernel memory from do_trap_ecall_u, causing a supervisor fault, corrupted control flow, and kernel oops or panic.

cna.title: riscv: entry: gate shadow call stack reload on sstatus.SPP, not tp

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

riscv: errata: select RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY for THEAD GHOSTWRITE

errata_probe_ghostwrite() only marks the CPU as vulnerable when it is
called at the RISCV_ALTERNATIVES_EARLY_BOOT stage, and the mitigation
in ghostwrite_enable_mitigation() only takes effect if the vulnerable
state was recorded before the boot alternatives are patched.

The early boot stage is only executed when CONFIG_RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY
is enabled, which currently is only selected by ERRATA_THEAD_MAE. In a
kernel built with ERRATA_THEAD_GHOSTWRITE=y but ERRATA_THEAD_MAE=n, the
early alternatives never run, so ghostwrite_state is never set to
VULNERABLE: ghostwrite_enable_mitigation() returns false, xtheadvector
remains enabled, and sysfs reports "Not affected" on a vulnerable
T-Head C9xx CPU.

Select RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY from ERRATA_THEAD_GHOSTWRITE so that the
vulnerability is detected in the early boot stage and the default
mitigation is applied.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A local process executes the GhostWrite vector sequence; its first vector instruction follows handle_exception() through do_trap_insn_illegal() to riscv_v_first_use_handler(), after which the faulty store executes in U-mode. No network protocol carries the causal input.
AC:H - Exposure requires a vulnerable T-Head C9xx with xtheadvector and the unusual build combination ERRATA_THEAD_GHOSTWRITE=y plus ERRATA_THEAD_MAE=n; both errata options default to y, and an attacker cannot create this kernel configuration.
PR:L - riscv_v_first_use_handler() and riscv_v_vstate_ctrl_set_current() contain no capability check, so an ordinary local user can enable vector state and execute the sequence; no administrative privilege or user namespace is required.
UI:N - The attacking process itself enables or first-uses vector state and executes the faulty store; no victim must mount media, open a file, or perform another action.
S:U - The missed disable_xtheadvector() call lets a user process escalate into the kernel on the same host; this is a local user-to-kernel privilege escalation under the host's existing security authority.
C:H - Leaving xtheadvector enabled exposes GhostWrite's arbitrary physical-write primitive; overwriting a PTE's page-frame number creates an arbitrary physical-read mapping covering kernel and other-process memory.
I:H - Because ghostwrite_enable_mitigation() returns false without the early VULNERABLE state, faulty high-order vector stores remain usable for attacker-chosen byte writes to physical memory, including PTEs and kernel or machine-mode code.
A:H - The same unrestricted physical writes can corrupt kernel text, page tables, or device MMIO, causing an unrecoverable kernel crash or system hang.

cna.title: riscv: errata: select RISCV_ALTERNATIVE_EARLY for THEAD GHOSTWRITE

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

riscv: futex: untag the user pointer before the atomic access

access_ok() checks untagged_addr(uaddr), but arch_futex_atomic_op_inuser()
and futex_atomic_cmpxchg_inatomic() hand the raw uaddr to the inline asm
amoswap/amoadd/.../lr.w+sc.w through the "+m" (*uaddr) operand.  When the
tagged address ABI is enabled (CONFIG_RISCV_ISA_SUPM, prctl
PR_SET_TAGGED_ADDR_CTRL with PMLEN != 0), those two addresses differ: a
user pointer whose top PMLEN bits hold a tag passes access_ok() after
untagging, but the atomic is then performed on the still-tagged raw
address.

Supervisor-mode data accesses are not subject to the U-mode pointer
masking (that is governed by menvcfg.PMM, which the kernel does not set),
so hardware does not strip the tag for the kernel's own access.  With
Sv57 and PMLEN=16 the tag bits overlap the canonical-address bits, so a
tagged pointer can name a canonical kernel virtual address (e.g. in the
linear map) whose untagged form is a valid user address.  An unprivileged
process can thus make FUTEX_WAKE_OP perform an atomic read-modify-write on
an arbitrary kernel address, with the matching FUTEX_OP_CMP_* result
serving as a read oracle.

get_user()/put_user()/raw_copy_{to,from}_user() already untag the pointer
after the access_ok() check; do the same in the futex helpers so the
atomic operates on the address that was actually validated.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - `sys_futex(FUTEX_WAKE_OP_PRIVATE)` follows `do_futex()` → `futex_wake_op()` → `futex_atomic_op_inuser()` → the patched `arch_futex_atomic_op_inuser()` using attacker-supplied `uaddr2`; no network data reaches this local syscall path.
AC:L - On an affected Sv57 system supporting PMLEN=16, the attacker deterministically enables tagged addresses with `prctl()` and supplies a canonical linear-map pointer; no race, victim state, or second actor is required.
PR:L - `sys_prctl(PR_SET_TAGGED_ADDR_CTRL)` and `sys_futex()` contain no capability or credential checks, so an ordinary unprivileged process can enable PMLEN=16 and invoke `FUTEX_WAKE_OP_PRIVATE`.
UI:N - The attacking process performs both `prctl()` setup and the futex operations itself; no victim must open, mount, approve, or otherwise act.
S:U - The AMO instructions corrupt the host kernel's own linear-map memory, producing ordinary local kernel privilege escalation without crossing a VM, IOMMU, or separate security authority.
C:H - The raw-address AMO returns the prior 32-bit kernel value to `futex_atomic_op_inuser()`, whose `FUTEX_OP_CMP_*` result can be observed through controlled waiters, providing a repeatable read oracle over direct-mapped physical memory.
I:H - `arch_futex_atomic_op_inuser()` executes `amoswap`, `amoadd`, `amoor`, `amoand`, or `amoxor` at the chosen kernel address; SET followed by shifted OR operations permits controlled 32-bit kernel-memory writes and privilege escalation.
A:H - The same chosen-address AMOs can overwrite direct-mapped kernel objects, credentials, or page-table memory; corrupting such live kernel state can reliably cause an oops, panic, or complete system failure.

cna.title: riscv: futex: untag the user pointer before the atomic access

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: hci_sync: Fix command skb lifetime during scan setup

During PA sync scan setup, hci_le_set_ext_scan_param_sync() gets the
address used for the PA_LINK lookup from hci_sent_cmd_data(). The
returned pointer borrows storage from sent_cmd or req_skb, without
holding a reference to either skb.

The scan worker runs on req_workqueue while hci_cmd_work() runs on the
separate device workqueue. After the scan worker loads sent_cmd, the
command worker can free and replace it before hci_sent_cmd_data()
dereferences the skb. The command payload can also be freed between
returning from the helper and comparing the address. The connection
lookup's RCU critical section does not protect the command skb.

KASAN reported:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in hci_sent_cmd_data+0x27c/0x2f0
  Workqueue: hci0 hci_cmd_sync_work
  Call Trace:
   hci_sent_cmd_data+0x27c/0x2f0
   hci_le_set_scan_param_sync+0x43a/0x850
   hci_passive_scan_sync+0xb09/0x1460
   hci_update_passive_scan_sync+0x47c/0x6e0
   hci_le_pa_create_sync+0x200/0xa70
   hci_cmd_sync_work+0x13c/0x290

  Allocated by task 95:
   skb_clone+0x13f/0x340
   hci_cmd_work+0x2a9/0x7e0

  Freed by task 95:
   kmem_cache_free+0xba/0x3a0
   hci_cmd_work+0x29c/0x7e0

Use hdev->lock to serialize the address snapshot with sent_cmd
replacement. Protect req_skb replacement and completion cleanup with
the same lock because the helper falls back to that skb. Copy the
address before releasing the lock and use the copy for the existing
RCU-protected connection lookup. Release the mutex before sending or
waiting for commands, preserving the lookup and completion ordering.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A local listen(2) on a broadcast BTPROTO_ISO socket reaches iso_sock_listen() → iso_listen_bis() → hci_pa_create_sync() → hci_le_pa_create_sync() → hci_le_set_ext_scan_param_sync(). No received Bluetooth PDU initiates this PA-sync setup.
AC:L - The attacker can run the ISO listen while flooding security-filter-permitted HCI_OP_READ_LOCAL_VERSION commands through a raw HCI socket; hci_sock_sendmsg() queues them on hdev->cmd_q, making hci_cmd_work() race hci_sent_cmd_data() on the separate req_workqueue.
PR:L - iso_sock_create(), bind(), and listen() have no capability check, while an unprivileged raw HCI socket may submit HCI_OP_READ_LOCAL_VERSION because OGF_INFO_PARAM/OCF 1 is in hci_sec_filter. Bluetooth sockets require init_net, but an ordinary host user satisfies that condition.
UI:N - The attacking process itself binds and listens on the broadcast ISO socket and submits the racing raw HCI commands; no separate victim action is needed once ISO sockets and the adapter are enabled.
S:U - The stale sent_cmd or req_skb and resulting memory access remain within the host kernel's Bluetooth authority; hci_le_set_ext_scan_param_sync() crosses no VM, IOMMU, or other security boundary.
C:H - hci_cmd_data() dereferences len and data from a freed sk_buff, and the returned command-payload pointer can itself be freed before the six-byte bdaddr read. Reclaiming the sprayable skbuff_head_cache object therefore supplies an attacker-directed stale-pointer read primitive.
I:H - A reclaimed command sk_buff controls the stale len/data fields and the bdaddr used to select a PA_LINK, whose iso_qos then determines the HCI_OP_LE_SET_EXT_SCAN_PARAMS command. This sprayable kernel use-after-free is an integrity-high memory-corruption primitive.
A:H - KASAN confirmed a slab-use-after-free in hci_sent_cmd_data(); dereferencing the freed sk_buff or its released payload can fault in hci_cmd_sync_work and cause a kernel oops or panic.

cna.title: Bluetooth: hci_sync: Fix command skb lifetime during scan setup
