In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: ISO: Reject concurrent BIS listener setup

iso_sock_listen() drops the socket lock before calling iso_listen_bis()
to preserve the hdev->lock ordering. Two concurrent listen() calls on
the same broadcast socket can therefore both observe BT_BOUND. Caller
A can attach connA and release the locks, then caller B can acquire
them and attach connB before A publishes BT_LISTEN.

__iso_chan_add() checks whether connB already has a socket, but not
whether the socket already has a connection. The second attachment
overwrites iso_pi(sk)->conn, leaking the connA reference and leaving
connA->sk intact. Socket teardown follows connB, so later events on
connA can cause a stale socket access.

Recheck BT_BOUND and require iso_pi(sk)->conn to be NULL after taking
both the HCI device and socket locks in iso_listen_bis(). The connection
check also covers the interval between attachment and publication of
BT_LISTEN. Reject a competing setup with -EBADFD through the existing
unlock path before allocating another connection.

A recorded KASAN report from an instrumented kernel shows:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in iso_sock_hold+0x119/0x1f0
  Call Trace:
   iso_sock_hold+0x119/0x1f0
   iso_conn_del+0xe4/0x270
   hci_disconn_complete_evt+0x351/0x8c0
   hci_event_packet+0x71b/0xb20
   hci_rx_work+0x293/0x730

  Allocated by task 93:
   sk_prot_alloc+0x113/0x220
   sk_alloc+0x2b/0x6d0
   bt_sock_alloc+0x29/0x370
   iso_sock_alloc.constprop.0+0x19/0x300
   iso_sock_create+0x94/0x100

  Freed by task 93:
   kfree+0x121/0x3c0
   __sk_destruct+0x42b/0x540
   iso_sock_release+0x29d/0x340
   __sock_release+0xa1/0x260
   sock_close+0x10/0x20

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The bad state is created by one process issuing two concurrent listen() syscalls on the same bound BTPROTO_ISO socket; __sys_listen_socket() reaches iso_sock_listen() and the patched iso_listen_bis(). An HCI disconnect only consumes the stranded connA->sk, so an adjacent peer cannot create the race alone.
AC:L - Attacker threads control both listen() calls and can make each observe BT_BOUND before either publishes BT_LISTEN, causing hci_pa_create_sync() to create separate candidates. The attacker can close the socket and end its own broadcast/sync to drive teardown, without victim-controlled timing.
PR:L - bt_sock_create(), iso_sock_create(), iso_sock_bind(), and iso_sock_listen() contain no capable() or ns_capable() check, so an ordinary process in init_net can create and race the socket. A separate network namespace is rejected, but no user namespace or capability is needed.
UI:N - The attacker creates and binds the ISO socket, launches both listen() calls, and closes it; the later HCI callback is asynchronous kernel/controller work. No victim action is required.
S:U - iso_conn_del() corrupts memory within the same host kernel that implements the attacker's ISO socket; the path crosses no VM, IOMMU, or other security authority boundary.
C:H - After iso_pi(sk)->conn is overwritten, connA retains connA->sk and iso_sock_hold() can refcount a freed or reclaimed kmalloc-2k struct iso_pinfo. Exploiting the ensuing callback-capable socket operations permits control-flow hijack and arbitrary kernel-memory disclosure.
I:H - iso_conn_del() passes the stale sk to iso_chan_del(), which writes sk_state and sk_err and invokes sk_state_change or parent->sk_data_ready. Reclaiming the freed object can turn these operations into arbitrary writes or control-flow hijacking.
A:H - KASAN observed the slab use-after-free in iso_sock_hold() from hci_disconn_complete_evt() after iso_sock_release() freed the socket. Invalid refcount, locking, and callback accesses can cause a kernel oops or panic.

cna.title: Bluetooth: ISO: Reject concurrent BIS listener setup

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: ISO: Serialize concurrent connect calls

iso_sock_connect() checks the socket state before taking the socket lock
and drops the lock again before setting up a connection. Two callers can
both pass the admission check while the socket is open or bound.

Caller A can copy its destination for route selection, then caller B can
replace the socket destination before A binds or connects the CIS. A
then uses B's destination with the route selected for its own request.
B can also proceed after A attaches a connection and sets BT_CONNECT.
For deferred BIS setup, B can bind a second BIS and overwrite
iso_pi(sk)->conn, leaving the first connection's reference and conn->sk
back-pointer stranded. Concurrent CIS connects can likewise replace the
socket's connection. Later teardown only detaches the current connection,
so a callback on the old connection can race with socket release and
access a freed socket.

KASAN reported:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in iso_sock_hold+0xf7/0x1b0
  Call Trace:
   iso_sock_hold+0xf7/0x1b0
   iso_conn_del+0x7b/0x1d0
   iso_connect_cfm+0x186/0x16a0
   hci_conn_failed+0x154/0x280
   hci_abort_conn_sync+0x3dc/0x7d0
   hci_cmd_sync_work+0x173/0x300

  Allocated by task 121:
   sk_alloc+0x2b/0x6d0
   bt_sock_alloc+0x29/0x370
   iso_sock_alloc.constprop.0+0x19/0x300
   iso_sock_create+0x94/0x100

  Freed by task 121:
   kfree+0x121/0x3c0
   __sk_destruct+0x42b/0x540
   iso_sock_release+0x29d/0x340
   __sock_release+0xa1/0x260

Check admission under the socket lock and mark the connect operation in
progress before publishing its destination. Keep that flag set across
route lookup and connection setup, rejecting another connect with
-EBADFD before it can change the destination or attach a connection.
Clear the flag after either helper returns, including on failure, so a
failed setup can be retried.

A separate flag is needed because the socket lock must be released before
acquiring the HCI device lock, while BT_CONNECT requires an attached
connection. Keep the existing state transitions and the deferred CIS
completion through iso_sock_recvmsg().

Reject an existing socket attachment in __iso_chan_add() before taking
a new reference or publishing either pointer, so every caller preserves
the connection association. Keep the same-socket, same-connection success
case for deferred CIS setup. Reject an attached socket before BIS setup
so a reusable BIS is not claimed before the attachment is rejected.

In CIS setup, reject a different HCI connection before iso_conn_add()
and drop the per-attempt HCI hold directly. An unowned iso_conn may still
carry another reference after detachment, so its destruction cannot be
relied on to release that hold.

iso_listen_bis() creates a fresh PA HCI/ISO pair under the device lock,
so the temporary iso_conn_put() frees the ISO candidate and drops its
HCI hold on rejection. iso_conn_ready() uses a freshly allocated,
unpublished child with no connection, making the socket-side rejection
unreachable.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The attack begins with two local connect(2) calls on one BTPROTO_ISO socket: __sys_connect() reaches iso_sock_connect(), whose pre-fix unlocked admission check lets both calls overwrite iso_pi(sk)->dst and attach different connections. No received Bluetooth message creates those concurrent calls or supplies the state that causes the overwrite.
AC:L - A process controls both sides by sharing one socket between threads and issuing concurrent nonblocking connects; the patched BT_SK_CONNECTING flag exists solely to serialize those calls. The stranded conn->sk persists until connection failure or abort, so the attacker can retry and close or spray sockets without depending on victim activity.
PR:L - bt_sock_create() and iso_sock_create() contain no capable() check, so an ordinary user in init_net can create the required AF_BLUETOOTH/SOCK_SEQPACKET/BTPROTO_ISO socket and call connect(). bt_sock_create() rejects non-initial network namespaces, but no administrative privilege is required in init_net.
UI:N - The attacker creates, races, and closes their own ISO socket; subsequent hci_conn_failed() -> iso_connect_cfm() -> iso_conn_del() teardown is automatic and needs no victim action.
S:U - The stale socket pointer is used and corrupted inside the host kernel's Bluetooth/socket memory, yielding an ordinary kernel compromise without crossing a VM, IOMMU, or separate security authority.
C:H - The overwrite leaves the old iso_conn->sk pointing at a freed, kmalloc-backed struct iso_pinfo; iso_conn_del() passes it through iso_sock_hold() and then reads socket, timer, connection, parent, and callback fields. Controlled heap reclamation makes this kernel UAF usable for high-impact memory disclosure.
I:H - Through stale conn->sk, iso_sock_hold() increments sk_refcnt and iso_conn_del()/iso_chan_del() manipulate the freed socket's lock, timer work, conn pointer, state, error, and callback. These writes into reclaimed heap memory support pointer/refcount corruption and control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The commit's KASAN trace demonstrates a slab use-after-free in iso_sock_hold() reached through hci_conn_failed() -> iso_connect_cfm() -> iso_conn_del(); dereferencing or locking the freed struct sock can oops or panic the kernel.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: SCO: serialise sco_conn lifetime against sco_recv_scodata()

sco_recv_scodata() upgrades the weak hcon->sco_data back-pointer to a
strong reference under hdev->lock:

    hci_dev_lock(hdev);
    hcon = hci_conn_hash_lookup_handle(hdev, handle);
    ...
    conn = sco_conn_hold_unless_zero(hcon->sco_data);
    hci_dev_unlock(hdev);

but the pointer is cleared from the other side without that lock. When
the last sco_conn reference is dropped, sco_conn_free() ran

    conn->hcon->sco_data = NULL;

with no hdev->lock held, so the RX path could read hcon->sco_data and
call kref_get_unless_zero() on an sco_conn that was concurrently freed:

    BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in sco_conn_hold_unless_zero+0xbe/0x160
    Write of size 4 by task kworker/u17:0
    Workqueue: hci0 hci_rx_work
    Call Trace:
     sco_conn_hold_unless_zero+0xbe/0x160
     sco_recv_scodata+0x13f/0x490
     hci_rx_work+0x3af/0x730

kref_get_unless_zero() only guards against a zero refcount, not against
the backing memory already being freed.

Give hcon->sco_data an actual reference on the sco_conn it points to, so
the object cannot be freed while the pointer is still installed, and only
clear and drop it from sco_conn_del(), which runs under hdev->lock (its
callers, sco_connect_cfm() and sco_disconn_cfm(), hold it). The reader in
sco_recv_scodata() also takes hdev->lock, so the store and the read are
now serialised: the RX path either observes NULL or a reference that is
guaranteed to stay valid until it drops its own.

sco_conn_add() no longer hands its kref_init() reference to the caller as
the connection's only reference; that initial reference is the one owned
by hcon->sco_data, and callers get their own via sco_conn_hold().

Because the sco_conn can now outlive the socket (the association keeps it
alive until the link goes down), the hci_conn can no longer be dropped
from sco_conn_free() without regressing socket close: closing a connected
SCO socket must still tear the link down. Move hci_conn ownership to the
socket instead: __sco_chan_add() takes an hci_conn reference and it is
released from sco_chan_del() and sco_sock_destruct(), exactly once. The
sco_conn no longer owns an hci_conn reference, so sco_conn_add() stops
consuming one and sco_connect() drops the hci_connect_sco() reference on
every path; sco_connect_cfm() no longer needs its hci_conn_hold() dance.

scenarios.value:
AV:A - An in-range peer's Bluetooth SCO/eSCO data enters as HCI_SCODATA_PKT through hci_recv_frame() → hci_rx_work() → hci_scodata_packet() → the patched sco_recv_scodata(). The radio-range transport makes the vector Adjacent.
AC:H - Peer-induced Disconnection Complete runs on the same ordered HCI workqueue and calls sco_conn_del() under hdev->lock, so it cannot create this race. Exploitation must instead coincide with local close()/shutdown() freeing the sco_conn outside that lock, timing the peer cannot control.
PR:N - hci_scodata_packet() and sco_recv_scodata() impose no peer credential or capability check once a SCO/eSCO handle exists. For inbound setup, sco_connect_ind() checks only for a listening SCO socket, not authentication.
UI:R - The last reference must be dropped through victim-side sco_sock_release() or sco_sock_shutdown() while peer data is received. Because peer-driven sco_disconn_cfm() is serialized against receive processing, a separate victim socket teardown is required.
S:U - The stale hcon->sco_data pointer corrupts a freed sco_conn inside the host Bluetooth kernel stack; it does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:H - After sco_conn_hold_unless_zero() revives reclaimed storage, sco_recv_frame() reads the reused conn->sk pointer and socket state. Heap grooming can therefore turn the sco_conn UAF into kernel-memory disclosure.
I:H - kref_get_unless_zero() performs a four-byte atomic increment in the freed sco_conn, followed on success by spinlock and kref operations on reclaimed storage. Reuse can convert these writes into kernel heap corruption and control-flow hijacking.
A:H - The demonstrated stale reference causes a KASAN slab-use-after-free write in sco_conn_hold_unless_zero() from hci_rx_work; such corruption can produce an oops or kernel panic.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/i915/gem: Prevent overstepping exec array boundary

It is possible for eb_relocate_parse_slow() to call kvfree() on
entries outside the original exec array during following
scenario inside eb_relocate_parse_slow():

1) eb_copy_relocations() allocates as many as eb->buffer_count
   copies for exec entries;
2) eb_parse() appends up to two VMAs, right after incrementing
   eb->buffer_count;
3) cleanup under "out" label uses this incremented buffer_count
   to release relocation pointers from exec array via kvfree(),
   not from VMA array.

To amend this problem, ensure that relocation cleanup uses the
original exec object count, excluding the VMAs appended by the
command parser.

(cherry picked from commit 2a0158925fb943c7ba8f3216e2734952128defc9)

scenarios.value:
AV:L - A local process reaches the patched cleanup through ioctl(2) → drm_ioctl() → i915_gem_execbuffer2_ioctl() → i915_gem_do_execbuffer() → eb_relocate_parse_slow(); the exec and relocation arrays originate in local userspace, not a wire protocol.
AC:L - On affected parser-enabled i915 hardware, the caller controls its relocs_ptr mapping to force eb_copy_relocations(), then submits a parser-using batch so eb_parse() appends VMAs. Any mapping race and heap grooming are controlled by the same caller and can be retried.
PR:L - I915_GEM_EXECBUFFER2_WR is registered with DRM_RENDER_ALLOW, and drm_ioctl_permit() imposes no DRM_AUTH, DRM_MASTER, DRM_ROOT_ONLY, or CAP_SYS_ADMIN check; an ordinary user with render-node access can invoke it.
UI:N - The attacker opens the i915 render node, prepares GEM objects and relocation arrays, and issues the execbuffer ioctl directly; no action by another user is required.
S:U - The erroneous kvfree() corrupts the host kernel heap from a host userspace client, constituting ordinary local-to-kernel escalation without crossing a VM, IOMMU, or other distinct security authority.
C:H - After eb_parse() increments buffer_count, eb_relocate_parse_slow() reads an untouched post-array slot as an exec object and passes its stale relocs_ptr to kvfree(); reusing a previously freed relocation-copy pointer produces a heap UAF capable of exposing kernel memory.
I:H - The attacker-groomable kvfree() can double-free or prematurely free a live allocation referenced through the stale relocs_ptr; reclaiming that object while stale users remain provides heap-corruption and control-flow-hijacking primitives.
A:H - kvfree() of the out-of-array relocs_ptr can immediately oops in kfree() for an invalid address or corrupt the allocator through a double-free; repeated execbuffer submissions can therefore crash or panic the kernel.

cna.title: drm/i915/gem: Prevent overstepping exec array boundary
